## A lie we have been telling

Last week we commanded joint angles and the robot went there. Mostly.

Look again at the Week 4 data: the pelvis was commanded to 0.72 m and never quite
arrived. Something between "the command" and "the motion" is not ideal, and this
week we open it up.

Three questions:

1. What *is* a position actuator, mechanically?
2. Why does the robot sag below its commanded height?
3. What happens when the motors are not strong enough?

The actuator is **declared in the model file** (Layer 2, the robot model), but
what it declares is a **controller** (Layer 4). This week sits on that seam.

---

## Colour code for the week {.smaller}

The same colours mean the same things in every equation and every drawing:

| symbol | meaning | unit | colour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${\color{#3b7dd8}{q,\ \dot q,\ \ddot q}}$ | the **joint angle**, its velocity, its acceleration | rad, rad/s, rad/s² | <span style="color:#3b7dd8">blue</span> |
| ${\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}}$ | the **command** — MuJoCo calls it `ctrl` | rad | <span style="color:#e8743b">orange</span> |
| ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau}}$ | a **torque** on the joint | N·m | <span style="color:#2a9d5c">green</span> |
| ${\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}$ | **stiffness**: torque per radian of error | N·m/rad | <span style="color:#c0392b">red</span> |
| ${\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}$ | **damping**: torque per rad/s of velocity | N·m·s/rad | <span style="color:#8e44ad">purple</span> |
| ${\color{#8c564b}{M}}$ | the **inertia** the joint has to swing | kg·m² | <span style="color:#8c564b">brown</span> |

Two derived numbers appear all week and are named when they arrive:
$\omega_n$ (how fast the joint responds) and $\zeta$ (whether it overshoots).

---

## The actuator is a controller in disguise {.smaller}

MuJoCo's "position actuator" is not a servo that magically achieves an angle. It
is a **PD controller** — proportional plus derivative — written into the model file:

$${\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau}} = {\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}\,({\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}) \;-\; {\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot{q}}}$$

- ${\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}$ — the **error**: how far the joint is from where it was told to be
- ${\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}\times$ error — the **P** term, a torque that pulls toward the command
- $-{\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot q}}$ — the **D** term, a torque that opposes motion, whichever way it goes

```{python}
try:
    import soc4180
except ImportError:
    %pip install -q "soc4180 @ git+https://github.com/gnoejh/soc4180.git"
    import soc4180

import numpy as np
import mujoco

model = soc4180.load_g1()
kp, kv = soc4180.gains(model)

print(f"kp : {np.unique(kp)}            (identical on every joint)")
print(f"kv : {kv.min():.2f} .. {kv.max():.2f}   ({len(np.unique(kv))} distinct values)")
```

**Stiffness is uniform; damping is not.** Heavier joints nearer the trunk carry
more damping. Why exactly that pattern is derived four slides from now.

---

## Where the gains live in the model {.smaller}

MuJoCo has one general formula for every actuator, and a `<position>` actuator
is just one choice of its numbers:

$${\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau}} = \underbrace{g_0}_{\texttt{gainprm[0]}}\,{\color{#e8743b}{\text{ctrl}}}
\;+\; \underbrace{b_0}_{\texttt{biasprm[0]}}
\;+\; \underbrace{b_1}_{\texttt{biasprm[1]}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}
\;+\; \underbrace{b_2}_{\texttt{biasprm[2]}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot q}}$$

Choose $g_0 = {\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}$, $b_0 = 0$, $b_1 = -{\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}$,
$b_2 = -{\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}$, collect terms, and it is the PD law of the last slide.

```{python}
a = 3                                    # actuator 3 is the left knee
print("actuator 3 :", mujoco.mj_id2name(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_ACTUATOR, a))
print(f"gainprm[0]      = {model.actuator_gainprm[a, 0]:+.3f}     (= +kp)")
print(f"biasprm[0:3]    = {np.round(model.actuator_biasprm[a, :3], 3)}   (= 0, -kp, -kv)")
```

That is why `soc4180.scale_gains` has to write **three** numbers per actuator:
$k_p$ appears twice. Change only the gain and the servo no longer pulls toward
`ctrl` — it pulls toward some other angle.

## The servo, drawn: a spring and a damper {.smaller}

```{python}

```

The left picture is a **sketch** (a sliding block standing in for a rotating
link: position ↔ angle, force ↔ torque, mass ↔ inertia). The spring is attached
to the *command*, so moving `ctrl` drags the spring's end; the damper is attached
to the *ground*, so it brakes any motion, even motion toward the target. The two
plots are the real knee's numbers: every 0.1 rad of error buys 50 N·m, and every
1 rad/s of speed costs 15.85 N·m of brake.

## One joint is a second-order system {.smaller}

Take one joint, gravity off, every other joint held still.

**Step 1 — Newton for rotation.** Inertia × angular acceleration = the torque on the joint:
$${\color{#8c564b}{M}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot q}} = {\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau}}.$$

**Step 2 — the only torque is the servo's.** Substitute the PD law:
$${\color{#8c564b}{M}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot q}} = {\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}({\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}) - {\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot q}}.$$

**Step 3 — collect the unknown on the left:**
$${\color{#8c564b}{M}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot q}} + {\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot q}} + {\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{q}} = {\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}\,{\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}}.$$

This is the **mass–spring–damper equation** — the most-studied equation in
engineering. It is *second order* because the highest derivative is $\ddot q$,
so we need two starting facts (angle and velocity) to know the future.

- ${\color{#8c564b}{M}}$ — the inertia of **everything beyond the joint** about its axis (the knee swings the shin and foot). MuJoCo computes it as the diagonal entry of the **mass matrix** `mj_fullM`, and adds the motor's own rotor inertia (`armature`, 0.01 kg·m² on every leg joint of the G1).
- The right-hand side is the **input**; the left-hand side is how the joint **responds**.

---

## Solving it: the characteristic equation {.smaller}

Command a **step**: ${\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}}$ jumps and then stays fixed. Write the error $e = {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}} - {\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}}$; since ${\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}}$ is constant, $\dot e = {\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot q}}$ and $\ddot e = {\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot q}}$, and the equation loses its right side:
$${\color{#8c564b}{M}}\,\ddot e + {\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}\,\dot e + {\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}\,e = 0 .$$

**Step 1 — try $e = e^{rt}$** (the same guess as Week 4's LIPM). Every term carries $e^{rt}$; cancel it:
$${\color{#8c564b}{M}}\,r^2 + {\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}\,r + {\color{#c0392b}{k_p}} = 0 .$$

**Step 2 — divide by ${\color{#8c564b}{M}}$ and name the two ratios:**
$$r^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n\,r + \omega_n^2 = 0,
\qquad \omega_n = \sqrt{\frac{{\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}}{{\color{#8c564b}{M}}}},
\qquad \zeta = \frac{{\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}}{2\sqrt{{\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}\,{\color{#8c564b}{M}}}} .$$
(Check: $\omega_n^2 = {\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}/{\color{#8c564b}{M}}$ and $2\zeta\omega_n = {\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}/{\color{#8c564b}{M}}$ — exactly the two coefficients.)

---

## The roots decide everything {.smaller}

**Step 3 — the quadratic formula** on $r^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n\,r + \omega_n^2 = 0$:
$$r = \omega_n\left(-\zeta \pm \sqrt{\zeta^2 - 1}\right).$$

- $\omega_n$ — the **natural frequency** (rad/s): how fast the joint would ring with no damping. Units: $\sqrt{(\text{N·m/rad})/(\text{kg·m}^2)} = 1/\text{s}$.
- $\zeta$ — the **damping ratio** (no unit). The square root decides everything: $\zeta < 1$ makes it imaginary, $\zeta = 1$ makes it zero, $\zeta > 1$ keeps it real.

**Step 4 — the solution is a sum of the two exponentials,** $e(t) = A\,e^{r_1 t} + B\,e^{r_2 t}$
(or $(A + Bt)\,e^{-\omega_n t}$ when the two roots coincide), with $A$ and $B$ fixed by the two starting facts: the step's size $e(0) = e_0$
(the error just after the jump) and $\dot e(0) = 0$ (the joint was at rest).
Both roots have negative real part whenever ${\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}} > 0$, so both
terms decay and **the joint always arrives** — the only question is *how*. The
next slide writes out $A e^{r_1 t} + B e^{r_2 t}$ for each case.

---

## Three regimes, three kinds of root {.smaller}

| | roots $r$ | error $e(t)$, starting at $e_0$ with zero velocity | what you see |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\zeta < 1$ **under-damped** | complex: $-\zeta\omega_n \pm i\,\omega_d$, $\ \omega_d = \omega_n\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$ | $e_0\,e^{-\zeta\omega_n t}\left(\cos\omega_d t + \dfrac{\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\sin\omega_d t\right)$ | rings: overshoots, swings back, decays |
| $\zeta = 1$ **critical** | one double root $-\omega_n$ | $e_0\,(1 + \omega_n t)\,e^{-\omega_n t}$ | fastest arrival **without** overshoot |
| $\zeta > 1$ **over-damped** | two real: $r_1, r_2 < 0$ | $e_0\,\dfrac{r_2 e^{r_1 t} - r_1 e^{r_2 t}}{r_2 - r_1}$ | creeps in; the slower root $r_1$ dominates |

A complex root $-a \pm i b$ means $e^{-at}$ (decay) times $\cos bt$ (oscillation):
that is where ringing comes from. Each formula was fitted to the two starting
facts, $e(0) = e_0$ and $\dot e(0) = 0$ — put $t = 0$ in and check.

---

## How much overshoot? {.smaller}

**Step 1 — find the peak.** For $\zeta < 1$, differentiate the error formula;
the cosine and sine terms combine and leave
$\dot e(t) = -e_0\,\dfrac{\omega_n}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\,e^{-\zeta\omega_n t}\sin\omega_d t$.
It is zero when $\sin\omega_d t = 0$, first at $t_p = \pi/\omega_d$.

**Step 2 — evaluate the error there.** Put $t_p$ into
$e_0\,e^{-\zeta\omega_n t}(\cos\omega_d t + \ldots\sin\omega_d t)$: $\cos\pi = -1$
and $\sin\pi = 0$, so $e(t_p) = -e_0\,e^{-\zeta\omega_n\pi/\omega_d}$. The minus
sign says the error has changed side: the joint is *past* the target.

**Step 3 — divide by the step and simplify** $\omega_n/\omega_d = 1/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}$:

$$\text{overshoot} = \frac{|e(t_p)|}{|e_0|} = e^{-\zeta\omega_n \pi/\omega_d} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{\pi\zeta}{\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}\right).$$

It depends on $\zeta$ **only**: $\zeta = 0.25$ gives 44 %, $\zeta = 0.5$ gives
16 %, and at $\zeta = 1$ the peak time $t_p = \pi/\omega_d$ becomes infinite —
no peak. **Stiffness sets the speed; the damping *ratio* sets the shape.**

---

## The three regimes, drawn for the knee {.smaller}

The left knee's numbers, with the damping scaled $\times\frac14$, $\times 1$, $\times 4$ — a 0.5 rad step:

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
d = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand"); mujoco.mj_forward(model, d)
M = np.zeros((model.nv, model.nv)); mujoco.mj_fullM(model, d, M)
dofs = model.jnt_dofadr[model.actuator_trnid[:, 0]]
M_knee = M[dofs[3], dofs[3]]

def second_order(t, zeta, wn, step=0.5):
    """The exact solution of M q'' + kv q' + kp q = kp q_ref, from rest, for a step."""
    if zeta < 1:
        wd = wn * np.sqrt(1 - zeta**2)
        e = np.exp(-zeta * wn * t) * (np.cos(wd * t) + zeta / np.sqrt(1 - zeta**2) * np.sin(wd * t))
    elif zeta == 1:
        e = (1 + wn * t) * np.exp(-wn * t)
    else:
        r1, r2 = wn * (-zeta + np.sqrt(zeta**2 - 1)), wn * (-zeta - np.sqrt(zeta**2 - 1))
        e = (r2 * np.exp(r1 * t) - r1 * np.exp(r2 * t)) / (r2 - r1)
    return step * (1 - e)

def first_within(t, q, target=0.5, tol=0.01):
    ok = np.abs(target - q) < tol * abs(target)
    return t[np.argmax(ok)] if ok.any() else float("nan")

wn = np.sqrt(kp[3] / M_knee)
t = np.linspace(0, 3.0, 30001)
fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 3.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.6, 1]})
th = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200); ax1.plot(wn * np.cos(th), wn * np.sin(th), ":", color="0.6")
print(f"knee: M = {M_knee:.4f} kg m^2, kp = {kp[3]:.0f}  ->  omega_n = {wn:.1f} rad/s = {wn / 2 / np.pi:.1f} Hz,"
      f" 1/omega_n = {1000 / wn:.1f} ms")
for kv_scale, col in ((0.25, "#e8743b"), (1.0, "k"), (4.0, "#3b7dd8")):
    zeta = kv[3] * kv_scale / (2 * np.sqrt(kp[3] * M_knee))
    zeta = round(zeta, 12)                     # 0.9999999999 is critical, not under-damped
    q = second_order(t, zeta, wn)
    lab = {0.25: "under", 1.0: "critical", 4.0: "over"}[kv_scale]
    ax0.plot(t, q, lw=2, color=col, label=fr"$\zeta$ = {zeta:.2f} ({lab}-damped)")
    roots = np.roots([1, 2 * zeta * wn, wn**2])
    ax1.plot(roots.real, roots.imag, "x", ms=10, mew=2.5, color=col)
    print(f"  kv x{kv_scale:<4}: zeta = {zeta:.2f}, roots = {np.round(roots, 1)}, "
          f"overshoot {max(q.max() - 0.5, 0) / 0.5:5.1%}, within 1 % after {first_within(t, q):.3f} s")
ax0.axhline(0.5, color="0.5", ls=":"); ax0.set_xlim(0, 0.5); ax0.set_xlabel("time after the step (s)")
ax0.set_ylabel("knee angle (rad)"); ax0.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right"); ax0.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax0.set_title("the exact solution, one-joint model", fontsize=10)
ax1.axhline(0, color="0.5", lw=0.8); ax1.axvline(0, color="0.5", lw=0.8)
ax1.set_xlim(-150, 30); ax1.set_ylim(-80, 80); ax1.set_aspect("equal")
ax1.annotate("other root\nat -497", xy=(-150, 0), xytext=(-140, 30), fontsize=8, color="#3b7dd8",
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#3b7dd8"))
ax1.set_xlabel("real part of $r$ (decay, 1/s)"); ax1.set_ylabel("imaginary part (ringing, rad/s)")
ax1.set_title(r"the roots; dotted: radius $\omega_n$", fontsize=10); ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

---

## Reading the numbers {.smaller}

- $\omega_n \approx 63$ rad/s, i.e. **10 Hz**: an undamped knee would ring ten
  times a second. $1/\omega_n \approx 16$ ms is the joint's basic time unit.
- **Critical ($\zeta = 1$, black):** both roots sit at $-\omega_n$, on the real
  axis — no ringing. It arrives within 1 % after 0.105 s. That is $6.64/\omega_n$,
  because $(1 + x)e^{-x} = 0.01$ at $x = 6.64$: about **seven time units**.
- **Under ($\zeta = 0.25$, orange):** the roots leave the axis, and the
  imaginary part (61 rad/s) is the ringing. Overshoot $\exp(-\pi\cdot0.25/\sqrt{1-0.0625}) = 44\%$.
  It gets *near* the target first (0.030 s) and then spends time swinging through it.
- **Over ($\zeta = 4$, blue):** two real roots, $-8$ and $-497$. The fast one
  dies in milliseconds; the slow one, $e^{-8t}$, is what you wait for: 0.577 s
  to reach 1 %, five times slower than critical.

**The circle.** A complex pair always has size exactly $\omega_n$:
$|r|^2 = (\zeta\omega_n)^2 + \omega_d^2 = \omega_n^2$. So below $\zeta = 1$ the damping
slides the pair *around* the circle towards the real axis; at $\zeta = 1$ they
meet on it at $-\omega_n$; above, they split along the axis, one inside and one
outside, with product $\omega_n^2$ ($8.0 \times 496.8 \approx 63.1^2$).
Stiffness sets the circle's size, damping sets where on it you are.

---

## What the G1's designers chose {.smaller}

Read ${\color{#8c564b}{M}}$ off the mass matrix for every actuated joint and compute $\zeta$:

```{python}
zeta = kv / (2 * np.sqrt(kp * M[dofs, dofs]))
for a in (0, 3, 4, 12, 16):
    name = mujoco.mj_id2name(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_ACTUATOR, a)
    print(f"  {name:26s} M = {M[dofs[a], dofs[a]]:.4f}   kv = {kv[a]:5.2f}   zeta = {zeta[a]:.2f}")
print(f"\nall twelve leg joints: zeta = {zeta[:12].min():.2f} .. {zeta[:12].max():.2f}")
```

**Every leg joint is critically damped, $\zeta = 1.00$.** That is why ${\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}$
varies by a factor of ten while ${\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}$ does not: solve $\zeta = 1$ for the damping,

$${\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}} = 2\sqrt{{\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}\,{\color{#8c564b}{M}}},$$

and a joint that swings more inertia needs more damping. The heavy hip and the
light ankle therefore respond with the *same shape*. The arms are looser, 0.7 to 1.9.

---

## The step response, measured {.smaller}

Gravity off, the robot lifted 0.5 m so nothing touches the floor, and the left
knee is asked to go from 0 to 0.5 rad. Solid: MuJoCo. Dashed: the one-joint formula.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
def step_response(kp_scale=1.0, kv_scale=1.0, seconds=0.5):
    m = soc4180.load_g1(); soc4180.scale_gains(m, kp_scale, kv_scale)
    m.opt.gravity[:] = 0
    d = soc4180.keyframe_data(m, "stand")
    d.qpos[2] += 0.5                                      # float clear of the floor
    mujoco.mj_forward(m, d)
    qi = m.jnt_qposadr[m.actuator_trnid[3, 0]]          # the left knee
    d.ctrl[3] = 0.5
    t0, t, q = d.time, [], []
    while d.time < t0 + seconds - 1e-9:
        mujoco.mj_step(m, d); t.append(d.time - t0); q.append(d.qpos[qi])
    return np.array(t), np.array(q)

def theory(t, kp_scale=1.0, kv_scale=1.0):
    z = round(kv[3] * kv_scale / (2 * np.sqrt(kp[3] * kp_scale * M_knee)), 12)
    return second_order(t, z, np.sqrt(kp[3] * kp_scale / M_knee)), z

fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.4), sharey=True)
rows = []
for ax, key, lab in ((ax0, "kp", r"$k_p$ = {:.0f}"), (ax1, "kv", r"$k_v \times$ {}")):
    for scale, col in ((0.25, "#e8743b"), (1.0, "k"), (4.0, "#3b7dd8")):
        kw = {f"{key}_scale": scale}
        t, q = step_response(**kw); qt, z = theory(t, **kw)
        ax.plot(t, q, lw=2, color=col, label=lab.format(500 * scale if key == "kp" else scale))
        ax.plot(t, qt, lw=1.2, ls="--", color=col)
        rows.append((f"{key} x{scale}", z, first_within(t, q), max(q.max() - 0.5, 0) / 0.5,
                     first_within(t, qt), max(qt.max() - 0.5, 0) / 0.5))
for ax, title in ((ax0, "stiffness sets how fast"), (ax1, "damping sets whether it overshoots")):
    ax.axhline(0.5, color="0.5", ls=":"); ax.set_xlabel("time after the step (s)")
    ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
ax0.set_ylabel("knee angle (rad)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"{'':9s} {'zeta':>5s} | {'MuJoCo: 1 %':>11s} {'overshoot':>9s} | {'formula: 1 %':>12s} {'overshoot':>9s}")
for r in rows:
    fmt = lambda x: "not yet" if np.isnan(x) else f"{x:.3f} s"
    print(f"{r[0]:9s} {r[1]:5.2f} | {fmt(r[2]):>11s} {r[3]:9.1%} | {fmt(r[4]):>12s} {r[5]:9.1%}")
```

---

## Reading the step response {.smaller}

- **Stiffness ×4** reaches 1 % in 0.032 s against 0.110 s — about 3.4 times
  sooner. Two things add up: $\omega_n \propto \sqrt{k_p}$ doubles, and
  $\zeta \propto 1/\sqrt{k_p}$ halves to 0.5, which rushes in and pays with a
  4.0 % overshoot. It also **draws four times the torque**: at the first
  instant the error is the whole 0.5 rad, so ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau}} = {\color{#c0392b}{k_p}} \times 0.5$ —
  250 N·m nominal, 1000 N·m at ×4.
- **A quarter of the stiffness, or four times the damping**, never gets within
  1 % in half a second ("not yet" in the table): over-damped, $\zeta = 2$ and $4$.
- **The nominal pair** is within 1 % at 0.110 s with no overshoot — the formula
  says 0.106 s (sampled every 2 ms, as MuJoCo is). $\zeta = 1$ predicted it.

But the under-damped cases **overshoot less than the formula says**: 16.9 %
measured against 44.4 % for ${\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}/4$. The next slide says why.

(The lab's `servo.py` prints smaller overshoots — 4.6 % for ${\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}/4$ —
because it starts with the feet on the floor and a foot touches it during the
step. This slide lifts the robot clear. Same law, different load.)

---

## Why the formula over-predicts the ringing {.smaller}

The one-joint model assumed "every other joint held still". The knee in a
floating robot does not push against a wall — it pushes against the rest of
the body, which moves back. Two limits bracket the truth:

```{python}
Minv = np.linalg.inv(M)
M_locked, M_free = M_knee, 1.0 / Minv[dofs[3], dofs[3]]
for label, m_ in (("every other joint locked   M_ii       ", M_locked),
                  ("every other joint free     1/(M^-1)_ii", M_free)):
    z = kv[3] / 4 / (2 * np.sqrt(kp[3] * m_))
    print(f"{label} = {m_:.4f} kg m^2 -> zeta(kv/4) = {z:.2f}, "
          f"overshoot {np.exp(-np.pi * z / np.sqrt(1 - z**2)):.1%}")
```

- ${\color{#8c564b}{M_{ii}}}$ (the diagonal) is the inertia when everything else is welded in place.
- $1/(M^{-1})_{ii}$ is the inertia when everything else — the other joints and the floating pelvis — is **perfectly free** to move out of the way. Less to push, so a smaller number and more damping per unit inertia.
- The real robot is in between: the other 28 joints are servoed, stiff but not rigid, and the pelvis floats. The measured 16.9 % is closer to the "free" limit, and even a little below it: a one-joint model, with either inertia, brackets the robot rather than fitting it.

**The formula is right about the direction and about the design rule** ($\zeta = 1$
gives no overshoot), and only approximate about the numbers. Use it to choose
gains; measure to know what you got.

---

## Verify it, do not believe it {.smaller}

If the PD law really is the actuator, we can predict the torque exactly:

```{python}
data = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand")
knee = soc4180.leg_qpos_indices(model, "left")[3]
data.qpos[knee] = 0.30          # bend the knee 0.3 rad away from the command
data.qvel[:] = 0                # no velocity, so the kv term vanishes
data.ctrl[:] = 0
mujoco.mj_forward(model, data)

a = 3                            # the left knee actuator
q = data.qpos[model.jnt_qposadr[model.actuator_trnid[a, 0]]]
predicted = kp[a] * (data.ctrl[a] - q)

print(f"predicted torque = {predicted:+.3f} N m")
print(f"actual   torque  = {data.actuator_force[a]:+.3f} N m")
```

Read it: error $0 - 0.30 = -0.30$ rad, times 500 N·m/rad, is $-150$ N·m — a
torque pulling the knee back toward straight. A spring, pulling the joint back
toward its setpoint with a force proportional to the error. **That is why the
robot sags: a spring at rest is a spring under load, and load means deflection.**

---

## Sag under gravity, derived {.smaller}

Turn gravity back on. Gravity pulls on everything beyond the joint and adds a
torque ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_g}}$ (MuJoCo's `qfrc_bias` with the sign flipped, when the robot is at rest):

**Step 1 — Newton with gravity:**
$${\color{#8c564b}{M}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot q}} = {\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}({\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}) - {\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot q}} + {\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_g}}.$$

**Step 2 — wait until it stops.** At rest ${\color{#3b7dd8}{\ddot q}} = {\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot q}} = 0$, so the damper does nothing and the spring alone holds the load:
$$0 = {\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}({\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}) + {\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_g}} .$$

**Step 3 — solve for the angle:**
$$\boxed{\ {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}} - {\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}} = \frac{{\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_g}}}{{\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}}\ }$$

---

## Reading the sag formula {.smaller}

$${\color{#3b7dd8}{q}} - {\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}} = \frac{{\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_g}}}{{\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}}$$

- The joint comes to rest **past** its command, in the direction gravity pulls, by load ÷ stiffness.
- Double ${\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}$, halve the sag. It is **never zero** for a finite spring: the error *is* what makes the holding torque.
- A PID controller would remove it with an integral (I) term that keeps growing while any error remains. MuJoCo's position actuator has no I term — the formula in *Where the gains live* has nothing that remembers the past.
- The G1's joints also have `frictionloss` 0.3 N·m, a small dead band: the spring may rest up to $0.3/{\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}$ either side of the prediction.

---

## Sag, measured on one joint {.smaller}

The robot stands; its left arm is held straight out in front (shoulder pitch
$-1.57$ rad, elbow 0). Only the shoulder's stiffness is changed:

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
names = [mujoco.mj_id2name(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_ACTUATOR, i) for i in range(model.nu)]
SH, EL = names.index("left_shoulder_pitch_joint"), names.index("left_elbow_joint")
ARM_OUT = -1.57

def arm_out(kp_scale=1.0, limit=None, seconds=3.0):
    m = soc4180.load_g1()
    k0 = m.actuator_gainprm[SH, 0]
    m.actuator_gainprm[SH, 0] = k0 * kp_scale; m.actuator_biasprm[SH, 1] = -k0 * kp_scale
    if limit is not None:                                  # a torque limit on this one motor
        m.actuator_forcelimited[SH] = 1; m.actuator_forcerange[SH] = [-limit, limit]
    d = soc4180.keyframe_data(m, "stand")
    qa = m.jnt_qposadr[m.actuator_trnid[[SH, EL], 0]]
    d.ctrl[[SH, EL]] = [ARM_OUT, 0.0]; d.qpos[qa] = [ARM_OUT, 0.0]
    mujoco.mj_forward(m, d)
    while d.time < seconds:
        mujoco.mj_step(m, d)
    tau_g = -d.qfrc_bias[m.jnt_dofadr[m.actuator_trnid[SH, 0]]]
    return d.qpos[qa[0]], tau_g, k0 * kp_scale

rows = [arm_out(s) for s in (0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0)]
body = lambda n: mujoco.mj_name2id(model, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_BODY, n)
d = soc4180.keyframe_data(model, "stand"); mujoco.mj_forward(model, d)
arm = np.linalg.norm(d.xpos[body("left_shoulder_pitch_link")] - d.xpos[body("left_wrist_yaw_link")])
print(f"{'kp':>6s} {'tau_g (N m)':>12s} {'predicted tau_g/kp':>19s} {'measured q - q_ref':>19s} {'wrist drop':>11s}")
for q, tg, k in rows:
    print(f"{k:6.0f} {tg:12.3f} {tg / k * 1000:15.2f} mrad {(q - ARM_OUT) * 1000:15.2f} mrad {(q - ARM_OUT) * arm * 1000:8.1f} mm")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 2.9))
kk = np.linspace(100, 2100, 200)
ax.plot(kk, rows[2][1] / kk * 1000, "--", color="0.5", label=r"$\tau_g / k_p$")
ax.plot([r[2] for r in rows], [(r[0] - ARM_OUT) * 1000 for r in rows], "o", ms=8, color="#3b7dd8", label="measured")
ax.set_xlabel("shoulder $k_p$ (N m/rad)"); ax.set_ylabel("sag (mrad)"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The arm (0.38 m from shoulder to wrist) pulls with 4.7 N·m. At the shipped
${\color{#c0392b}{k_p}} = 500$ it sags 9.5 mrad — half a degree, 3.6 mm at the
wrist — and every point lands on $\tau_g/k_p$ to within 0.05 mrad.

---

## Measure the sag {.smaller}

The same law, for a whole walking robot:

```{python}
from soc4180.walking import WalkingController, GaitParams

controller = WalkingController(model, GaitParams(n_steps=8))
data = controller.initial_data()

sag, peak = [], 0.0
while data.time < controller.total_time:
    data.ctrl[:] = controller.control(data.time)
    mujoco.mj_step(model, data)
    peak = max(peak, float(np.abs(data.actuator_force).max()))
    if data.time > controller.params.settle_time:
        sag.append(controller.targets_at(data.time)[0][2] - data.qpos[2])

print(f"commanded pelvis height : {controller.params.pelvis_height:.3f} m")
print(f"mean sag                : {np.mean(sag)*1000:+.1f} mm")
print(f"worst sag               : {np.max(sag)*1000:+.1f} mm")
print(f"peak joint torque       : {peak:.1f} N m")
```

Eleven millimetres of steady droop. Not a bug — the necessary deflection of
finite springs holding up a 33 kg robot. Each leg joint sags by its own
$\tau_g/k_p$, and the pelvis drop is those small angles added up along the leg.

---

## Sag against stiffness {.smaller}

The derivation says sag $\propto 1/k_p$. Sweep the stiffness of **every** joint and check:

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
def walk_sag(kp_scale):
    m = soc4180.load_g1(); soc4180.scale_gains(m, kp_scale, 1.0)
    c = WalkingController(m, GaitParams(n_steps=8)); d = c.initial_data(); s = []
    while d.time < c.total_time:
        d.ctrl[:] = c.control(d.time); mujoco.mj_step(m, d)
        if d.time > c.params.settle_time:
            s.append(c.targets_at(d.time)[0][2] - d.qpos[2])
    return np.mean(s) * 1000, d.qpos[2]

scales = np.array([0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0])
sags, ok = [], []
for s in scales:
    mm, z = walk_sag(s); sags.append(mm); ok.append(z > 0.5)
sags, ok = np.array(sags), np.array(ok)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.4))
ax.plot(500 * scales[ok], sags[ok], "o", ms=8, color="#3b7dd8", label="walked: mean sag")
ax.plot(500 * scales[~ok], np.zeros((~ok).sum()), "x", ms=10, mew=2, color="#e8743b", label="fell")
kk = np.linspace(400, 1100, 100)
ax.plot(kk, sags[1] * 500 / kk, "--", color="0.5", label=r"$\propto 1/k_p$ through the nominal point")
ax.set_xlabel("$k_p$"); ax.set_ylabel("mean pelvis sag (mm)"); ax.set_ylim(bottom=-1)
ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("  ".join(f"kp {500 * s:.0f}: {'%.1f mm' % mm if o else 'fell'}" for s, mm, o in zip(scales, sags, ok)))
```

500 and 600 sit on the $1/k_p$ curve; 750 sags a little less than it
predicts (6.0 mm against 7.3) — the pelvis sag is many joints at once, each
at its own load, so the single-spring law is a guide, not a fit. Below 500 the robot does
not sag more — it **falls**: a leg that gives too much at support exchange has
stopped supporting. Above 750 it falls too, for the reason on the next slides —
the gait's timing was tuned against one particular stiffness.

---

## The motors in this model are infinitely strong {.smaller}

Before tuning anything, check what the simulator is actually giving us:

```{python}
print(f"torque limit in the model : {soc4180.torque_limit(model)}")
print(f"control limits set?       : {bool(np.any(model.actuator_ctrllimited))}")
```

**`None`.** The MJCF constrains the *commanded angle* to the joint range, but
places no bound whatsoever on the torque used to get there. Our walker happily
drew 124 N·m peaks and nothing objected.

No real motor behaves like this. Every hardware actuator has a stall torque, a
thermal limit, and a gearbox that fails. **This is a sim-to-real gap sitting in
plain sight in the model file**, and unlike most of them it costs one line to
close.

---

## Saturation, written as maths {.smaller}

A torque limit ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_{\max}}}$ clips the PD law:

$${\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau}} = \operatorname{clip}\!\Big({\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}({\color{#e8743b}{q_{\text{ref}}}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{q}}) - {\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}\,{\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot q}},\; -{\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_{\max}}},\; +{\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_{\max}}}\Big)$$

($\operatorname{clip}(x, lo, hi)$ returns $x$ if it is between the bounds, otherwise the bound it crossed.)

**Step 1 — where the spring is still a spring.** At rest, the law is linear only while
$|{\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}\,e| \le {\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_{\max}}}$, i.e.
$$|e| \le \frac{{\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_{\max}}}}{{\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}} = \frac{50}{500} = 0.1\ \text{rad} \approx 5.7° \quad\text{(for a 50 N·m limit)}.$$

**Step 2 — outside that band the stiffness is zero.** The torque is stuck at
${\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_{\max}}}$: more error buys no more torque, so nothing
pulls harder as the joint falls further. Everything derived so far ($\omega_n$, $\zeta$, the sag) assumed the linear band.

**Step 3 — holding a load.** The sag formula needs $|{\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_g}}| \le {\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_{\max}}}$.
If gravity asks for more, **no value of ${\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}$ helps**: the joint
gives way until gravity's own torque has fallen to ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_{\max}}}$ —
for an arm, until it hangs low enough that its lever arm is shorter.

---

## A weak shoulder, measured {.smaller}

The straight-out arm again, with a torque limit on the shoulder motor alone.
Green: gravity's torque at each angle (`mj_forward`, no simulation).

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
m = soc4180.load_g1(); d = soc4180.keyframe_data(m, "stand")
qa = m.jnt_qposadr[m.actuator_trnid[[SH, EL], 0]]; sh_dof = m.jnt_dofadr[m.actuator_trnid[SH, 0]]
angles = np.linspace(ARM_OUT, 0.5, 600); tg = []
for a_ in angles:
    d.qpos[qa] = [a_, 0.0]; mujoco.mj_forward(m, d); tg.append(-d.qfrc_bias[sh_dof])
tg = np.array(tg)
FRICTION = m.dof_frictionloss[sh_dof]                      # can hold either way
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 2.7))
ax.plot(np.degrees(angles), tg, color="#2a9d5c", lw=2, label=r"gravity torque $\tau_g$ at the shoulder")
print(f"gravity's largest pull on the straight arm: {tg.max():.2f} N m;  joint friction {FRICTION:.1f} N m")
first = lambda mask: np.degrees(angles[np.argmax(mask)]) if mask.any() else float("nan")
for lim, col in ((6.0, "0.4"), (4.0, "#e8743b"), (3.0, "#c0392b"), (2.0, "#8e44ad")):
    q_end, _, _ = arm_out(limit=lim, seconds=4.0)
    ax.axhline(lim, color=col, ls=":", lw=1)
    ax.plot(np.degrees(q_end), lim, "o", ms=8, color=col)
    if tg.max() <= lim:
        print(f"  limit {lim:.0f} N m: stronger than gravity everywhere -> holds; measured {np.degrees(q_end):6.1f} deg")
        continue
    lo, hi = first(tg <= lim + FRICTION), first(tg <= lim - FRICTION)
    ax.plot([lo, hi if np.isfinite(hi) else 28.6], [lim, lim], lw=6, alpha=0.25, color=col, solid_capstyle="butt")
    print(f"  limit {lim:.0f} N m: predicted rest between {lo:6.1f} and {hi:6.1f} deg, measured {np.degrees(q_end):6.1f} deg")
ax.set_xlabel("shoulder pitch (deg);  -90 = straight out,  0 = hanging"); ax.set_ylabel("torque (N m)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.set_title("dotted: the limit; band: rest predicted within the friction; dot: measured rest", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

6 N·m beats gravity's largest pull (5.09): the arm holds. Weaker, it gives way
and stops where $\tau_g$ has fallen to the limit — a band, not a point, because
the 0.3 N·m joint friction holds either way. 4 and 3 N·m land in their bands;
2 N·m stops 0.4° short. **Stiffness never entered**: past saturation, only ${\color{#2a9d5c}{\tau_{\max}}}$ matters.

---

## Close it and find the breaking point {.smaller}

```{python}
def walks(torque_limit=None, kp_scale=1.0, kv_scale=1.0, n_steps=8):
    m = soc4180.load_g1()
    soc4180.scale_gains(m, kp_scale, kv_scale)
    soc4180.set_torque_limit(m, torque_limit)
    c = WalkingController(m, GaitParams(n_steps=n_steps))
    d = c.initial_data()
    while d.time < c.total_time:
        d.ctrl[:] = c.control(d.time)
        mujoco.mj_step(m, d)
    return float(d.qpos[0]), float(d.qpos[2])

for limit in (30, 45, 50, 55, 80, None):
    x, z = walks(torque_limit=limit)
    tag = "no limit" if limit is None else f"{limit:3d} N m"
    print(f"  {tag:9s} -> travelled {x:+.3f} m, pelvis {z:.3f} m   "
          f"{'FELL' if z < 0.5 else 'walked'}")
```

A crisp threshold: the gait **needs more than 50 N·m** and survives at 55. Below
that the stance leg cannot hold the robot up during weight transfer, and it goes
down.

---

## Where the torque goes {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
m = soc4180.load_g1()
c = WalkingController(m, GaitParams(n_steps=8)); d = c.initial_data()
tt, tau = [], []
while d.time < c.total_time:
    d.ctrl[:] = c.control(d.time); mujoco.mj_step(m, d)
    tt.append(d.time); tau.append(d.actuator_force.copy())
tt, tau = np.array(tt), np.abs(np.array(tau))
names = [mujoco.mj_id2name(m, mujoco.mjtObj.mjOBJ_ACTUATOR, i).replace("_joint", "")
         for i in range(m.nu)]
peak_tau = tau.max(axis=0)

fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.6), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.5, 1]})
ax0.plot(tt, tau[:, 3], lw=1, color="#3b7dd8", label="left knee")
ax0.plot(tt, tau[:, 9], lw=1, color="#e8743b", label="right knee")
for lim, ls in ((50, "--"), (55, ":")):
    ax0.axhline(lim, color="k", ls=ls, lw=1); ax0.text(0.1, lim + 2, f"{lim} N m", fontsize=8)
ax0.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax0.set_ylabel("|knee torque| (N m)")
ax0.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right"); ax0.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax0.set_title("the knees during the walk", fontsize=10)
order = np.argsort(peak_tau)[::-1][:8]
ax1.barh([names[i] for i in order], peak_tau[order], color="#3b7dd8"); ax1.invert_yaxis()
ax1.axvline(50, color="k", ls="--", lw=1); ax1.set_xlabel("peak |torque| (N m)"); ax1.grid(axis="x", alpha=0.3)
ax1.set_title("the eight loudest actuators", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"left knee above 50 N m for {(tau[:, 3] > 50).mean():.1%} of the walk")
```

The knee holds the body up in single support and spikes at every support
exchange. (The 124 N·m spike at $t \approx 0$ is the robot landing from its
starting pose, before walking begins.) It exceeds 50 N·m for about **4% of the walk** — and that is enough.
In those moments the knee is outside its linear band (Step 2 of the saturation
slide): it stops being a spring, extra bending meets no extra torque,
and a limit that bites for a few hundredths of a second drops the robot.

---

## Tuning the gains {.smaller}

${\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}$ too low and the robot sinks. Too high and it fights itself. Find the window:

```{python}
for scale in (0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0):
    x, z = walks(kp_scale=scale)
    print(f"  kp = {500*scale:6.0f} -> travelled {x:+.3f} m, pelvis {z:.3f} m   "
          f"{'FELL' if z < 0.5 else 'walked'}")
```

**Only the nominal gain walks.** Halve it and the legs collapse under the robot's
weight; double it and the servos overpower the gait's timing and throw it over.

---

## The textbook fix that does not work {.smaller}

The derivation says the *shape* of the response depends only on
$\zeta = {\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}} / (2\sqrt{{\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}\,{\color{#8c564b}{M}}})$.
So scale ${\color{#8e44ad}{k_v}}$ by $\sqrt{s}$ whenever ${\color{#c0392b}{k_p}}$ is scaled by $s$,
and $\zeta$ stays exactly 1.00 on every leg joint. Try it:

```{python}
for scale in (0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0):
    x, z = walks(kp_scale=scale, kv_scale=np.sqrt(scale))
    print(f"  kp = {500*scale:6.0f}, kv x{np.sqrt(scale):.2f} -> "
          f"pelvis {z:.3f} m   {'FELL' if z < 0.5 else 'walked'}")
```

**Still only the nominal gain survives.** The theory is not wrong — it is about a
single joint tracking a setpoint. Holding $\zeta$ keeps the *shape* but changes
the *speed* ($\omega_n \propto \sqrt{k_p}$) and the *sag* ($\propto 1/k_p$). Our
failure is not one joint ringing; it is a *whole-body gait whose timing was
tuned against this particular plant*. Change the plant and the trajectory no
longer fits it.

Remember that when a learned policy shrugs this off in Week 11.

---

## Rhythm without a model {.smaller}

The Week 4 walker needed a balance model. Biology often seems not to: a **central
pattern generator** (CPG) — a circuit of neurons in the spinal cord — produces
rhythmic stepping with no plan at all. Two anti-phase oscillators, driving hips and knees:

```{python}
cpg = soc4180.CPG(model, frequency=1.2, hip_amplitude=0.25, knee_amplitude=0.40)
data = cpg.initial_data()
frames = soc4180.render_rollout(
    model, data, duration=8.0, fps=30, width=560, height=440,
    ctrl_fn=cpg.ctrl_fn(), track="pelvis", distance=2.6, azimuth=135,
)
print(f"after 8 s: x={data.qpos[0]:+.3f} m, pelvis {data.qpos[2]:.3f} m")
soc4180.show_video(frames, fps=30)
```

---

## A CPG is coupled oscillators {.smaller}

Give each leg a **phase** ${\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi}}$ (blue here: the state; ${\color{#8e44ad}{w}}$ purple: the coupling) (radians, going round and
round: $\phi$ and $\phi + 2\pi$ are the same moment of the stride). Each phase
advances at its own rate and is **nudged** by the other:

$${\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot\phi_L}} = \omega_L + {\color{#8e44ad}{w}}\sin({\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi_R}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi_L}} - \pi),
\qquad
{\color{#3b7dd8}{\dot\phi_R}} = \omega_R + {\color{#8e44ad}{w}}\sin({\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi_L}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi_R}} + \pi)$$

- $\omega_L, \omega_R$ — each leg's own stepping rate, $2\pi f$ (rad/s); $f$ = stride cycles per second
- ${\color{#8e44ad}{w}}$ — the **coupling** strength (1/s): how hard each leg pulls the other's phase
- $\pi$ — the **desired phase offset**: the legs half a stride apart, i.e. alternating

**Step 1 — watch the phase error** $e = {\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi_R}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi_L}} - \pi$. Subtract the two equations (note $\phi_L - \phi_R + \pi = -e$):
$$\dot e = (\omega_R - \omega_L) - 2{\color{#8e44ad}{w}}\sin e .$$

One equation in one unknown: the whole two-leg question is now "where does $e$ go?"

---

## Why the legs lock {.smaller}

$$\dot e = (\omega_R - \omega_L) - 2{\color{#8e44ad}{w}}\sin e, \qquad e = {\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi_R}} - {\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi_L}} - \pi$$

**Step 2 — equal rates.** $\dot e = -2{\color{#8e44ad}{w}}\sin e$. Near $e = 0$, $\sin e \approx e$, so $e(t) = e_0\,e^{-2wt}$ — the same kind of decaying exponential as the servo. The legs **lock into anti-phase**, the error shrinking by a factor $\mathrm{e} \approx 2.72$ every $1/(2w)$ seconds. $e = \pi$ (both legs together — a hop) is also a rest point, but an unstable one: there $\sin e \approx -(e - \pi)$ pushes away.

**Step 3 — unequal rates**, $\Delta\omega = \omega_R - \omega_L$. The error stops where $\dot e = 0$: $\sin e^* = \Delta\omega / 2w$. That has a solution **only if $|\Delta\omega| \le 2w$** — coupling strong enough to overrule the mismatch locks the legs with a small lag $e^*$; weaker coupling lets them drift apart for ever.

---

## Coupled oscillators, drawn {.smaller}

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
def phase_error(e0, w, dw, f=1.2, seconds=4.0, dt=1e-3):
    """Integrate the two phase equations (Euler) and return t and the wrapped error e."""
    pL, pR = 0.0, e0 + np.pi
    wL, wR = 2 * np.pi * f, 2 * np.pi * f + dw
    ts, es = [], []
    for k in range(int(seconds / dt)):
        dL = wL + w * np.sin(pR - pL - np.pi); dR = wR + w * np.sin(pL - pR + np.pi)
        pL += dL * dt; pR += dR * dt
        ts.append(k * dt); es.append(np.angle(np.exp(1j * (pR - pL - np.pi))))
    return np.array(ts), np.array(es)

fig, (ax0, ax1) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 3.4))
for e0 in (-3.0, -1.5, 0.5, 2.0, 3.1):
    t, e = phase_error(e0, w=2.0, dw=0.0)
    ax0.plot(t, e, lw=1.8)
ax0.axhline(0, color="k", ls=":"); ax0.set_ylim(-np.pi - 0.2, np.pi + 0.2)
ax0.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax0.set_ylabel(r"phase error $e$ (rad)"); ax0.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax0.set_title(r"equal rates, $w$ = 2/s: every start locks to $e = 0$", fontsize=10)
dw = 2 * np.pi * 0.1
for w, col in ((2.0, "#3b7dd8"), (0.25, "#e8743b")):
    t, e = phase_error(0.0, w=w, dw=dw, seconds=12.0)
    ax1.plot(t, e, lw=1.8, color=col, label=f"$w$ = {w}/s  ($2w$ = {2 * w:.2f})")
    pred = np.arcsin(dw / (2 * w)) if dw <= 2 * w else float("nan")
    print(f"w = {w:4}: 2w = {2*w:.2f} vs mismatch {dw:.3f} rad/s -> predicted lag {pred:.3f} rad, "
          f"measured e after 12 s = {e[-1]:+.3f} rad")
ax1.set_ylim(-np.pi - 0.2, np.pi + 0.2); ax1.set_xlabel("time (s)"); ax1.grid(alpha=0.3); ax1.legend(fontsize=8)
ax1.set_title(r"right leg 0.1 Hz faster ($\Delta\omega$ = 0.63 rad/s)", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
t, e = phase_error(0.5, w=2.0, dw=0.0)
print(f"equal rates, w = 2: e went 0.500 -> {e[int(0.25 / 1e-3)]:.3f} rad after 1/(2w) = 0.25 s "
      f"(the formula says {0.5 * np.exp(-1):.3f})")
```

Left: whatever the starting error, the legs settle half a stride apart within
about a second — the start near $e = \pi$ (a hop) lingers longest before
tipping off the unstable point. Right: with strong coupling (blue) the faster
leg is held back and the pair locks with a small constant lag; with weak
coupling (orange) the error wraps round and round: the legs drift in and out of step.

---

## What the oscillator commands {.smaller}

The package's `soc4180.CPG` uses the **locked solution directly**: equal rates,
$e = 0$ from the start, so ${\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi_L}} = 2\pi f t$ and
${\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi_R}} = {\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi_L}} + \pi$ with no coupling term to compute —
nothing ever disturbs an open-loop clock. Each phase is turned into joint targets
(added to the Week 4 crouch):

$$\theta_{\text{hip}} = A_h \sin{\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi}},\qquad
\theta_{\text{knee}} = A_k \max(0, \sin{\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi}}),\qquad
\theta_{\text{ankle}} = -\tfrac{1}{2} A_h \sin{\color{#3b7dd8}{\phi}}$$

- $A_h$ (`hip_amplitude`, 0.25 rad) swings the thigh forward and back
- $A_k$ (`knee_amplitude`, 0.40 rad) bends the knee only on the forward half: $\max(0, \cdot)$ cuts off the negative half, since a knee cannot bend backward
- the ankle counter-rotates by half the hip swing to keep the foot roughly level

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
from soc4180 import kinematics as kin
tt = np.linspace(0, 2.0, 400)
idx = {s: kin.leg_qpos_indices(model, s) for s in ("left", "right")}
act_q = np.array([model.jnt_qposadr[model.actuator_trnid[a, 0]] for a in range(model.nu)])
cmd = np.array([cpg.control(cpg.settle_time + t) for t in tt])       # actuator order
full = np.tile(cpg.nominal, (len(tt), 1)); full[:, act_q] = cmd
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8.4, 3.4), sharex=True)
for ax, side in zip(axs, ("left", "right")):
    i = idx[side]
    for j, lab, col in ((0, "hip pitch", "#3b7dd8"), (3, "knee", "#e8743b"), (4, "ankle pitch", "#2a9d5c")):
        ax.plot(tt, full[:, i[j]] - cpg.nominal[i[j]], lw=2, color=col, label=lab)
    ax.set_ylabel(f"{side} (rad)"); ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
axs[0].legend(fontsize=8, ncol=3, loc="upper right"); axs[1].set_xlabel("time (s)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

A perfectly plausible stepping pattern. It also has no idea where the floor is.

---

## Rhythm is not balance {.smaller}

Three stepping rates × three amplitude pairs, 8 s each:

```{python}
for f in (0.8, 1.2, 1.6):
    row = []
    for h, k in ((0.15, 0.25), (0.25, 0.40), (0.35, 0.55)):
        c = soc4180.CPG(model, frequency=f, hip_amplitude=h, knee_amplitude=k)
        d = c.initial_data(); fell = None
        while d.time < 8.0:
            d.ctrl[:] = c.control(d.time); mujoco.mj_step(model, d)
            if fell is None and d.qpos[2] < 0.5:
                fell = d.time
        row.append(f"A=({h:.2f},{k:.2f}): " + (f"fell at {fell:.1f} s" if fell else "upright"))
    print(f"{f} Hz   " + "   ".join(row))
```

**All nine fall, between 1.9 and 3.2 seconds in.** The legs move in a
perfectly good walking pattern. Nothing keeps the centre of mass over the
support polygon, so the robot walks its legs and falls anyway.

**This is the value of Week 4 stated negatively.** The LIPM was not decoration;
it was the entire reason the robot stayed up.

---

## What biology actually does

Real CPGs are not open loop. In an animal the rhythm is continuously **entrained
by sensory feedback** — load on the leg, joint angle, skin contact — through
reflex pathways that adjust the pattern step by step. In the phase equations
that is one more term: $\dot\phi = \omega + (\text{coupling}) + (\text{feedback})$,
and a feedback term that speeds up or holds back one leg's phase is exactly the
kind of disturbance Step 3 says the coupling can absorb.

An open-loop oscillator is a CPG with its spinal cord cut off from its body.

That is precisely what we are missing, and it names the next two weeks:

- **Week 6** — read the sensors: what can the robot actually know about itself?
- **Weeks 8+** — let a policy learn the feedback rule instead of deriving it

---

## Where this leaves us {.smaller}

| | LIPM walker (W4) | CPG (today) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model of balance | yes | none |
| Walks | yes, ~1 m | no |
| Sensors used | none | none |
| Survives gain changes | no | no |
| Lines of code | ~200 | ~20 |

Both are **open loop**. Neither reads a single sensor. One works because a human
did the balance reasoning in advance; the other does not work at all.

Every remaining week of the course is about closing that loop.

Holds `stand`, jumps one joint's target, prints the law by hand against

replays. `--walk` runs the gait under the new gains instead.

| gains | ζ | 1 % reached | overshoot | peak torque |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| as shipped | 1.00 | 0.132 s | 0.1 % | 250 N·m |
| kp × 4 | 0.50 | 0.036 s | 2.1 % | 1000 N·m |
| kv / 4 | 0.25 | 0.034 s | 4.6 % | 250 N·m |

| Step | Does | Calls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | scale gains, set the limit | `scale_gains`, `set_torque_limit` |
| 2 | ζ = kv / 2√(kp M) | `mj_fullM`, `jnt_dofadr[actuator_trnid]` |
| 3 | the step or the walk | `ctrl`, `mj_step`, `actuator_force`, `targets_at` |
| 6 | replay | `launch_viewer(passive=True)` |

## Exercises {.smaller}

1. **Bisect the torque limit.** Narrow the walking threshold between 50 and
   55 N·m to 1 N·m. Which joint saturates first, and during which gait phase?
2. **Sag versus stiffness.** Plot mean sag against $k_p$ over the range that does
   not fall. Is the relationship $1/k_p$ as a linear spring predicts?
3. **Compensate it.** The sag is ~11 mm and roughly constant. Raise the commanded
   pelvis height by that amount and re-measure. Does the tracking error vanish,
   and does anything else get worse?
4. **Damping alone.** Hold $k_p$ fixed and sweep $k_v$ over 0.25×–4×. Which
   failure looks like ringing and which like sluggishness?
5. **Give the CPG a reflex.** Increase knee amplitude on whichever leg carries
   more load (read `data.actuator_force`). Does one feedback term save it?
6. **Cost of transport.** Compute $\int |\tau \dot q|\,dt$ per metre for the
   Week 4 walker. Keep the number — you will compare a learned policy against it.
7. **Overshoot from the formula.** Using the knee's $M_{ii}$ and the free-body
   $1/(M^{-1})_{ii}$, predict the overshoot for $k_v \times 0.5$, then measure
   it with the lifted step response. Which limit is closer?
8. **Lock the legs.** In `phase_error`, find the weakest coupling $w$ that
   still locks a 0.2 Hz mismatch, from Step 3, and check it by simulation.
